perspective:
Harold’s available information:

- He is Harold Padilla, a project manager. He feels frustrated and anxious because he believes his project team is unmotivated and project progress is suffering.
- He knows Arthur Begum as a police officer friend/colleague whose advice he trusts. Harold arranges and attends a coffee-shop meeting with Arthur.
- At that meeting, Harold tells Arthur the team seems unmotivated and he is at his wit’s end. He hears Arthur suggest understanding each team member’s individual motivation and having one-on-one conversations. Harold decides to try this and feels hopeful/relieved.
- Harold tells his team he wants one-on-one chats to understand what motivates them. He hears Team Member 1 say that could be helpful and Team Member 2 say they are open to it. Harold plans to schedule the chats.
- Later, Harold observes the team still not responding well. He feels disappointed and worried. He tells Arthur his suggestions did not work. He hears Arthur suggest deeper issues may be involved, such as personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors, and that he may need to dig deeper. Harold decides to set up another round of meetings.
- Harold becomes determined/focused. In one-on-one meetings, he asks team members to share concerns or problems. He hears Team Member 1 report tension among a few people affecting work. He hears Team Member 2 report feeling overwhelmed by the workload and stressed.
- Harold tells them he will look into resolving conflicts and possibly redistribute tasks, and that their well-being is important.
- Harold feels optimistic/empowered. He tells the team they will have regular feedback sessions and team-building activities. He hears Team Member 1 say that sounds great and should help, and Team Member 2 agree that their concerns are being addressed. Harold says he is glad and wants to work together, emphasizing their input and well-being.
